title: Arshdeep Singh Dang Becomes First Sikh RAF Fighter Pilot Since World War II
excerpt: The Indian-origin flight lieutenant, born in Chandigarh and raised in the UK, graduated as a fast jet pilot at RAF Valley in North Wales, fulfilling his late grandfather's dream.
body:
• Flight Lieutenant Arshdeep Singh Dang has become the first Sikh to graduate as a fighter pilot in Britain's Royal Air Force since World War II.
  • Dang, 28, was born in Chandigarh and moved to the UK at age six. He studied mathematics and philosophy at the University of Bristol before joining the RAF.
  • The RAF announced the milestone at a fast jet pilot graduation ceremony at RAF Valley in North Wales on August 14.
  • Dang's achievement continues a legacy that stretches back to Hardit Singh Malik in World War I and Mohinder Singh Pujji in World War II.

A Family Dream Takes Flight

Indian-origin Flight Lieutenant Arshdeep Singh Dang has become the first Sikh to graduate as a fighter pilot in the Royal Air Force since World War II, the RAF announced at a fast jet pilot graduation ceremony at RAF Valley in North Wales on August 14.

https://x.com/WIONews/status/2088993822814699642

For Dang, the achievement carries deeply personal weight. His paternal grandfather, Sardar Santokh Singh Dang, had dreamed of seeing his son become a pilot — but died when Dang's father was just six years old.

"My grandfather died when my father was just 6. So my father never really had those opportunities or resources to fulfil his wish. My parents encouraged me, and I started to believe that I could be a pilot. And it happened."

— Arshdeep Singh Dang, speaking to The Indian Express

Dang was born in Chandigarh in 1998. His father, Jagdeep Singh Dang, is from Ludhiana, and his mother, Gagandeep Kaur, is from Amritsar. The family moved to the United Kingdom when Arshdeep was six years old. He went on to study mathematics and philosophy at the University of Bristol before pursuing a military flying career.

Years of Training

Dang's path to fighter wings spanned several stages. He completed RAF officer training in February 2022, followed by elementary flying training in 2023. After serving in Cyprus, he was selected for the fast-jet stream in 2024.

His fast jet lead-in training began in March 2025, with basic fast-jet training starting in July of that year. In October 2025, Dang flew solo in Texas — a landmark stage in the fast-jet pipeline. He successfully passed his wings test in July 2026.

Even with fighter wings now earned, Dang faces approximately another year of intensive training before progressing to frontline fighter aircraft.

Continuing a Historic Legacy

The RAF described Dang's graduation as the first time since World War II that a Sikh has attained fighter wings from a fighter squadron. The milestone connects to a distinguished but little-known history of Sikh military aviators in British service.

Hardit Singh Malik became the first Indian to fly as a pilot with the Royal Flying Corps — the RAF's predecessor — during World War I. Known as the "Flying Sikh," Malik wore a specially designed helmet over his turban and flew Sopwith Camel combat missions across France and Italy. He survived being shot down, his aircraft riddled with over 450 bullet holes.

During World War II, Squadron Leader Mohinder Singh Pujji volunteered for the RAF and flew combat missions across Europe, North Africa, and Burma. Pujji was one of roughly 24 Indian volunteers who served in the RAF during the war. He was awarded the Distinguished Flying Cross for heroism, including helping rescue 300 American troops in Burma.

After Pujji's generation, no Sikh had earned RAF fighter wings — until Dang.

Inspiring the Next Generation

Speaking to The Indian Express, Dang said he felt privileged to represent his community on an international stage. He expressed the hope that he would not be the last Sikh to reach this milestone, saying he wanted his accomplishment to inspire others to pursue military aviation regardless of their background.

Dang's story resonates across the Indian diaspora in Britain, where Sikhs have a long but often overlooked history of military service. An estimated 83,000 Sikh soldiers of the British Indian Army were killed serving in the two World Wars, with another 109,000 wounded — a contribution now marked by memorials across the UK, including a statue of Hardit Singh Malik in Southampton.
